# TPUs Are Finally for Sale, But Why?

- URL: https://haifengjin.com/tpus-are-finally-for-sale-but-why/
- Date: 2026-10-30
- Subtitle: An analysis of Google's entry into the AI chip market

Ever since Google first unveiled its custom Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) in 2016[@tpu-announcement][@tpu-v1-paper], the hardware was guarded like a crown jewel. For a full decade, Google maintained an unbroken rule that not a single data center TPU was allowed to leave its proprietary data centers. The silicon was exceptionally powerful, yet the only way external developers could ever touch it was by renting virtual machines through Google Cloud Platform. Outside of Google's walled garden, these TPUs simply did not exist.

Now, that ten-year doctrine has suddenly collapsed. Google Cloud officially confirmed a historic strategic shift, announcing that it is deploying TPU hardware directly inside external, third-party data centers, beginning with a major partnership to bring TPUs to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure[@google-tpu-oracle].

In this article, we revisit why Google held back for so long, analyze the financial realities driving its sudden reversal, evaluate the structural advantages it brings to the AI chip market, explore the technical co-design implications for open-source AI development, and weigh the challenges ahead.

DISCLAIMER: The views expressed in this article are solely those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the opinions or viewpoints of Google or its affiliates. The entirety of the information presented within this article is sourced exclusively from publicly available materials.

## What happened?

In an official announcement, Google Cloud confirmed that it is bringing physical TPU hardware into Oracle Cloud Infrastructure data centers[@google-tpu-oracle]. Crucially, this is not just another way to rent compute on Google Cloud Platform. The hardware will be installed outside Google-operated infrastructure and run within Oracle facilities, letting customers access Google silicon without migrating their existing data center architecture.

The announcement follows Alphabet's second-quarter 2026 earnings disclosures, where management highlighted surging demand from compute-intensive sectors, including frontier AI labs, quantitative finance firms, and high-performance computing centers[@alphabet-tpu-sales]. While major labs like Anthropic have long relied on Google Cloud TPUs[@anthropic-tpu], physically deploying silicon inside external operators marks an entirely new chapter for Google.

## Why didn't Google do this earlier?

In our previous [blog post](/tpus-are-not-for-sale-but-why/), we discussed why Google doesn't sell TPUs. The TPU project was originally created strictly for Google's own internal services rather than as a commercial silicon product. Adapting the hardware and software for third-party deployments would have demanded substantial extra work[@semianalysis-tpuv7]. Following the launch of ChatGPT, Google chose to direct its resources toward closing the model capability gap with OpenAI, staying laser-focused on model quality rather than taking on the distraction and operational overhead of supporting external hardware clients.

However, things are different now. Google has steadily improved its model intelligence and closed the capability gap with OpenAI. When Gemini 3 Pro debuted in late 2025, it claimed the number one spot on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index[@artificial-analysis][@gemini-3-pro-model-card]. Even as rival labs pushed out newer models, Google maintained its standing at the frontier. The later release of Gemini 4 Argon[@gemini-4-argon] reinforced Google's position among the elite tier of frontier reasoning models. With its models now performing at the highest tier across industry benchmarks, frontier model development no longer demands the company's undivided defensive focus.

## The financial pressure

The main driver behind selling TPUs directly is financial reality. Big tech companies like Google, Microsoft, Amazon, and Meta are all aggressively expanding their data center footprints[@reuters-ai-capex] to meet a surge in inference demand, with token consumption projected to grow exponentially in the coming years[@semianalysis-tokenomics]. However, building massive AI data centers requires staggering amounts of capital expenditure. In the second quarter of 2026, Google's free cash flow fell under severe pressure, dipping into negative territory as quarterly capital expenditures surged to unprecedented levels to build out this compute infrastructure[@alphabet-q2-2026-results].

Google needs new revenue streams to boost its cash flow. In the AI industry, one of the most lucrative business models right now is selling chips. For now, buyers can often make the hardware pay for itself simply by setting up hosted inference services and selling tokens directly on platforms like OpenRouter[@openrouter]. Remarkably, even with token prices among the lowest in the industry, economic estimates from DeepSeek's operational disclosures suggest hardware procurement costs can be recouped in as little as 10 months at high utilization[@deepseek-payback]. Because short payback cycles make compute clusters financially attractive even under aggressive token pricing, buyers have continued to aggressively snap up available hardware capacity across the market[@patel-payback]. By selling physical TPU systems directly to customers, Google can tap into that high-margin hardware revenue stream.

## Google's built-in advantages

Google enters the field with substantial advantages. It brings battle-tested scale, enterprise distribution, and cost flexibility.

First, its silicon is already proven at immense scale. Google trains its Gemini models entirely on TPUs, and Anthropic officially uses Google Cloud TPUs to train and deploy its models[@anthropic-tpu]. Meta has also reportedly held talks to rent TPU capacity and eventually deploy TPUs in its own data centers[@meta-tpu-talks]. Few chips outside Nvidia's lineup can claim this level of frontier adoption.

This widespread adoption across frontier labs means much more than just a proof of reliability. Running cutting-edge workloads directly drives the hardware's evolution. As frontier architectures push against memory bandwidth, latency, and interconnect limits, chip design iterates hand-in-hand with model development. Google does not build silicon in a vacuum and hope algorithms adapt to it. Instead, TPUs have evolved through years of tight co-design with the demands of state-of-the-art models.

This tight feedback loop is critical in modern AI. It is a key reason why Nvidia builds in-house models like Nemotron[@nemotron-4] to ensure its architecture teams have a proprietary co-design loop to optimize future GPUs.

Second, Google has a built-in distribution channel. Unlike a pure hardware startup trying to sign its first customers, Google can seamlessly tap into its massive base of existing enterprise cloud accounts. Google already manages the billing, relationships, and deployment tooling for thousands of organizations, giving it direct access to buyers who already run core workloads within the Google ecosystem.

Third, Google benefits from absorbed R&D costs and exceptional pricing flexibility. The company does not need to load the heavy historical development costs of TPUs onto external customers. Because Google has operated and scaled the TPU program for internal workloads over a full decade without selling a single data center chip, the foundational engineering has already been amortized by Google's core revenue engines, including Search, Ads, YouTube, and Gemini. As long as the selling price exceeds the marginal cost of manufacturing the hardware, Google can price aggressively while still generating attractive margins and positive cash flow, though every chip sold externally is one fewer chip for its own workloads.

## The broader technical impact

Whether or not community influence was Google's primary motive, putting physical TPUs into customer data centers carries massive technical implications for the open-source ecosystem.

Hardware vendors care intensely about how well open-weight models run on their silicon. A major segment of hardware buyers purchases compute specifically to run inference on these models. Buyers naturally gravitate toward whichever architecture runs open models the fastest and cheapest to keep operational costs low. For hardware makers, championing open-weight ecosystems directly fuels silicon sales. Nvidia's acquisition of HuggingFace[@nvidia-huggingface] and an open letter it backed advocating for open-weight models[@open-weights-letter] reflect these commercial incentives.

Crucially, modern open-source models tend to overfit the hardware they are developed on. Inference optimization does not only happen after training finishes. Model builders also tailor the neural network architecture for hardware efficiency from the very start, choosing layer shapes and dimensions before training ever begins. Because inference serving costs dictate whether developers and enterprises can afford to deploy a model at scale, optimizing for the target hardware from the beginning gives a model a major head start in efficiency and adoption.

For example, Nvidia designed Nemotron-4 340B[@nemotron-4] with an attention head dimension of 192. During attention computation, this results in matrix multiplications involving a key dimension of 192. Nvidia Tensor Cores process these operations by tiling matrices into small sub-blocks of 16 by 16 or 64 by 64. Because 192 is an exact multiple of these tile sizes (three 64-wide blocks), the dimension maps cleanly onto the GPU's tile sizes without padding.

In contrast, the Matrix Multiply Units (MXUs) on TPU v5 and earlier execute operations using fixed 128 by 128 systolic arrays[@tpu-performance-guide]. When tiling a dimension of 192, the TPU fills one full 128-wide tile, leaving a remaining tile of 64. The compiler must pad that remaining 64 with zeros to complete the 128-wide array, running the hardware unit at only half capacity for that chunk.

This zero-padding wastes a quarter of the MXU's work on every attention matmul that runs over the head dimension, lowering the goodput of the TPU. As a result, Nemotron-4 runs less efficiently out of the box on TPUs, and closing the gap with Nvidia GPUs takes extra engineering effort.

This tiling mismatch is only one example of how modern architectures overfit Nvidia hardware. Across the industry, model dimensions are often chosen with Nvidia GPU Tensor Core utilization in mind, while novel mathematical operations are frequently abandoned if they cannot be fused into efficient CUDA kernels. Much of the open-source tooling, from GPU-centric kernel languages like Triton[@triton-paper] to low-precision formats like Nvidia's NVFP4 on Blackwell[@nvfp4-paper], is built first and foremost to extract maximum performance from GPUs.

This creates a powerful flywheel for the ecosystem moat Google wants to build. When open models are developed on TPUs, they run faster on Google silicon out of the box. Buyers choose TPUs to run those models at the lowest cost, driving hardware adoption. More TPUs in the wild in turn motivate developers to build on Google silicon, locking in a self-reinforcing advantage.

Currently, that same flywheel works against Google because popular open models are already tailored for Nvidia GPUs. To kickstart its own flywheel, Google must take the initiative to bridge this gap, optimizing leading open models for TPUs and demonstrating that they run just as fast and cost-effectively on its hardware.

## The challenges ahead

Selling hardware directly to customers brings two major challenges Google has never had to navigate at this scale.

The first is balancing internal compute needs against hardware sales. Google DeepMind requires massive TPU capacity to train and serve Gemini models. Because chip supply and packaging capacity are limited, Google must carefully balance how many chips it sells to customers against the compute it keeps for itself, ensuring near-term hardware revenue does not slow down its own model development.

The second challenge is customer trust. Pure-play foundries like TSMC succeeded in chip manufacturing because they promised never to compete with their customers in chip design. Google, on the other hand, builds both the hardware and the frontier models that directly compete with its buyers. To win over enterprise buyers, Google must earn their long-term trust, proving it will reliably supply the latest silicon in sufficient volume rather than hoarding its best chips to gain a competitive advantage over its customers.

## Summary

Google's decision to finally sell physical TPUs comes down mostly to money. Building out AI infrastructure costs a fortune, and surging capital spending just pushed Google's free cash flow into negative territory. Selling expensive AI chips directly to customers brings in fast, high-margin revenue to help foot the bill.

Google is in a great spot to do this. Its chips already help power frontier models like Gemini and Claude, its enterprise sales network is already up and running, and its R&D costs have long been paid for by products like Google Search and YouTube.

Yet succeeding as a merchant hardware vendor will test Google in new ways. It must balance selling chips externally against preserving enough compute for its own Gemini models, while proving to customer-competitors that it will be a reliable, trustworthy partner rather than a rival hoarding the best hardware for itself.

For the rest of the AI world, this could shake things up. The open-source community has been stuck on Nvidia GPUs for years because today's models are built around them. If Google puts the work in to make popular open models run smoothly on TPUs, it can kickstart a flywheel that gives developers more choices and real competition in AI hardware.

# The Anatomy of an LLM

- URL: https://haifengjin.com/the-anatomy-of-an-llm/
- Date: 2026-09-06
- Subtitle: Every tensor operation explained with code and diagrams

In this article, we walk through every tensor operation in a modern large
language model (LLM). For an ML systems engineer, mastering the exact compute
graph is a must-have for optimizing training and inference performance, whereas
the statistical theory and modeling assumptions are often secondary. When both
are taught together, the abstract math often obscures the mechanical reality.

The same thing happens on the implementation side. Squeezing code into as few
lines as possible makes it cryptic, while piling on hardware-specific
performance optimizations quickly buries the core architecture under complex
engineering tricks. That is why our implementation does not optimize for lines
of code or raw runtime performance. Instead, it optimizes strictly for
readability at the compute level, while remaining mathematically equivalent to
heavily optimized production systems.

To reduce cognitive load, this article keeps the math to a strict minimum,
using visual diagrams and clean Python code to trace how every tensor moves
through the model. All code is available in the open-source
[readable-llm](https://github.com/haifeng-jin/readable-llm) repository, which
implements every operation in pure Python with zero dependencies. At the end
of the article, we also put everything together in a
[complete computation graph](/the-anatomy-of-an-llm/graph/) so you can visually
explore the end-to-end flow.

## LLMs have evolved

Over the past few years, the Transformer architecture has evolved significantly
beyond the original "Attention Is All You Need" paper[@attention-is-all-you-need].
Several key techniques have been introduced and widely adopted as the modern standard,
including the decoder-only architecture[@gpt], Mixture of Experts (MoE)[@moe],
Grouped-Query Attention (GQA)[@gqa], Root Mean Square Normalization (RMSNorm)[@rmsnorm],
and Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE)[@rope]. The architecture we walk through here
adopts all of these modern techniques.

## pipeline

Let's start with an end-to-end abstraction of an LLM pipeline in the following
figure. We input a question, and the pipeline appends the answer to the string.
Note that we simplified the text by omitting special tokens and chat template
markers here (such as `<bos>`, `<start_of_turn>`, and `<eos>`), which models use
to mark the start and end of questions and responses.

Throughout the article, we use a single input prompt instance with no batch
dimension for simplicity. Most operations process this sequence directly, except
for a few cases in the MoE module where we further split that down to a single
token.

Notice that `pipeline` is drawn as a capsule. Throughout this article, a capsule
represents a module with internal structure and states that we will further
break down.

[Diagram: The end-to-end pipeline receives a raw text prompt and returns the completed text response. (llm/pipeline.svg)]

As shown in the figure below, the pipeline breaks down into three parts:
`tokenizer.encode`, `model.generate`, and `tokenizer.decode`. Let's walk through them one by one.
Notice the small capsule in the top-right corner of the diagram, which shows
which module we are currently breaking down.

[Diagram: The pipeline capsule breaks down into three sequential submodules. (llm/pipeline-breakdown.svg)]

Here is what `pipeline` looks like in Python:

```python
def pipeline(prompt, tokenizer, model):
    # input_ids: [seq_len]
    input_ids = tokenizer.encode(prompt)
    # output_ids: [total_seq_len]
    output_ids = model.generate(input_ids)
    # output_text: string
    output_text = tokenizer.decode(output_ids)
    return output_text
```

## tokenizer.encode

The job of a tokenizer is to convert between text strings and lists of integer
token IDs. Let's see how that works in practice.

In the figure below, `tokenizer.encode` turns the input text into a list of token
IDs. To keep things simple, we can imagine that each word or punctuation mark is
its own token, though modern tokenizers usually split text into subword pieces.
The tokenizer first chops the string into individual tokens (like `['What', ' is', ' 1', '+', '1', '?']`),
and then looks each one up in a dictionary that maps tokens to unique integers.

[Diagram: tokenizer.encode splits the prompt string into tokens and maps each token to an integer ID. (llm/encode-output.svg)]

The lookup table (or vocabulary) maps each token string to its assigned ID. It
contains all the possible tokens that the LLM can speak:

```python
vocab = {
    "+": 10,
    "1": 16,
    "?": 30,
    " is": 318,
    " 1": 352,
    "What": 1867,
    # ...
}
```

Notice why the two `1`s in our prompt get different IDs (`352` and `16`):
tokenizers treat whitespace as part of the token, so `' 1'` (with a
leading space) and `'1'` (without) get distinct entries. That is also why
`' is'` carries its space. Decoding is then a plain string join, with no need
to guess where the spaces went.

Here is what `tokenizer.encode` looks like in Python:

```python
class Tokenizer:
    def __init__(self, vocab):
        self.vocab = vocab
        self.inv_vocab = {token_id: token for token, token_id in vocab.items()}

    def encode(self, text):
        tokens = split_tokens(text)
        # input_ids: [seq_len]
        input_ids = [self.vocab[token] for token in tokens]
        return input_ids
```

Notice that `__init__` also builds `self.inv_vocab`. This is an inverted
dictionary that flips the keys and values, mapping each integer token ID back to
its string token. We don't need it inside `encode`, but it will be used in
`tokenizer.decode` to turn generated token IDs back into text.

We use `seq_len` (sequence length) to describe the number of tokens in this sequence.
This dimension will appear in tensor shapes throughout the rest of the model.

## tokenizer.decode

Similarly, `tokenizer.decode` takes the full ID sequence (the original prompt
plus any newly generated tokens) and converts it back into text, using the
inverted lookup table `inv_vocab` we built earlier:

[Diagram: tokenizer.decode takes the full sequence of token IDs and converts them back into text. (llm/decode-input.svg)]

Here is what `tokenizer.decode` looks like in Python:

```python
class Tokenizer:
    # ...
    def decode(self, token_ids):
        # token_ids: [seq_len]
        return "".join(self.inv_vocab[token_id] for token_id in token_ids)
```

## model.generate

`model.generate` is the module that generates new token IDs and appends them
to the sequence, as shown in the figure below.

[Diagram: model.generate takes the prompt token IDs and returns the complete token sequence. (llm/generate-io.svg)]

Those new tokens are generated one by one by `greedy_sampler`. With each step,
the input sequence grows by one token as the newly predicted ID is appended:

[Diagram: Inside model.generate, greedy_sampler predicts one token ID per step, which is appended to the sequence to form the input for the next step. (llm/predict-growth.svg)]

At each step, `model.generate` calls `greedy_sampler` to predict the next token,
appends that token to the sequence, and feeds the longer sequence back in. This
loop continues until the model produces an end-of-sequence token or reaches a
maximum length limit.

Here is what the generation loop looks like in Python:

```python
MAX_NEW_TOKENS = 128
EOS_TOKEN_ID = 2

class Model:
    # ...
    def generate(self, input_ids):
        # input_ids: [seq_len]
        for _ in range(MAX_NEW_TOKENS):
            # next_token_id: int
            next_token_id = greedy_sampler(self, input_ids)
            # input_ids: [seq_len + 1]
            input_ids = input_ids + [next_token_id]
            if next_token_id == EOS_TOKEN_ID:
                break
        # input_ids: [total_seq_len]
        return input_ids
```

## greedy_sampler

We use greedy sampling here for simplicity. In practice, modern LLMs typically
rely on stochastic sampling techniques like temperature scaling, top-$p$
(nucleus) sampling, and top-$k$ sampling to generate more diverse and creative
responses instead of always picking the single most probable token.

In a single call to `greedy_sampler`, `model.predict` turns `input_ids`
into `logits`, and then `argmax` (marked as **A** in the diagram) picks the
highest-scoring token ID. While capsules represent modules with internal
structure and states, circles in our diagrams represent pure functions with no
internal states:

[Diagram: In a single step of greedy_sampler, model.predict turns input_ids into logits (scores), and argmax selects the highest-scoring next_token_id. (llm/sampler-step.svg)]

Each number in the `logits` vector represents the score for the token associated
with that index. So the size of the vector is `vocab_size`, exactly one score
for each token in the vocabulary. For example, `logits[318]` is the score for
token ID 318, which corresponds to the string `' is'` in our vocabulary. `argmax`
simply picks whichever token ID has the highest score.

Here is what `argmax` looks like in Python:

```python
def argmax(logits):
    # logits: [vocab_size]
    # max_idx: int
    max_idx = 0
    for i in range(len(logits)):
        if logits[i] > logits[max_idx]:
            max_idx = i
    return max_idx
```

Putting it together, here is what `greedy_sampler` looks like in Python:

```python
def greedy_sampler(model, input_ids):
    # input_ids: [seq_len]
    # logits: [vocab_size]
    logits = model.predict(input_ids)
    # next_token_id: int
    next_token_id = argmax(logits)
    return next_token_id
```

## model.predict

Now, we are ready to further break down `model.predict` into smaller components.
`model.predict` is the step that actually calls the neural network model. It
runs one forward pass of it.

It turns the `input_ids` into the logits for the next token across the
vocabulary. It breaks down into three parts: `embedding`, `decoder`,
and `lm_head`, as shown in the figure below.

[Diagram: model.predict breaks down into three core submodules. (llm/predict-breakdown.svg)]

Here is what `model.predict` looks like in Python:

```python
class Model:
    # ...
    def predict(self, input_ids):
        # input_ids: [seq_len]
        # embed_out: [seq_len, hidden_size]
        embed_out = self.embedding(input_ids)
        # decoder_out: [seq_len, hidden_size]
        decoder_out = self.decoder(embed_out)
        # logits: [vocab_size]
        logits = self.lm_head(decoder_out)
        return logits
```

Now, we will tackle the three components one by one. We will explore `embedding`
and `lm_head` first before diving into the more complex `decoder`.


## embedding

Zooming into the `embedding` module, it takes `input_ids` as input and maps each
integer ID to a vector of floating-point numbers, producing the matrix
`embed_out`:

[Diagram: The embedding module maps integer token IDs to dense vectors, producing the 2D embed_out matrix. (llm/embedding-breakdown.svg)]

Note that `embed_out` is the end of the backward pass during training. Because
token IDs are discrete integers, gradients cannot backpropagate any further
into the input text. Gradients update the weights in `embedding_table`, and
backpropagation stops there.

`embedding` is a token-wise operation, which means it processes each token in
isolation. No token depends on the value or position of other tokens to pass
through this module. As shown in the figure below, we can conceptually split the
sequence into individual tokens, process each one independently, and combine the
vectors back together to form `embed_out`:

[Diagram: model.predict -> embedding<br>Inside embedding, each token ID selects its corresponding row from embedding_table via lookup (circled L) to form embed_out. (llm/embedding-internals.svg)]

A few quick notes here:
1. Splitting into individual tokens is purely for illustration. Real hardware
   does not loop through tokens one by one in Python; modern frameworks look up
   the entire sequence at once in parallel via batched tensor indexing
   (`embedding_table[input_ids]`).
2. Most operations in an LLM are token-wise. The attention layer in the decoder
   blocks is the sole exception where tokens actually interact with one another.
3. The blue box represents learnable weights. Here, `embedding_table` holds the
   model parameters updated during training. We will use this same blue style
   for all weights throughout the rest of the diagrams to distinguish them from
   intermediate activations (shown with white backgrounds).

During the lookup, each token ID indexes into `embedding_table` of shape
`[vocab_size, hidden_size]`, where each row is an embedding vector corresponding
to one specific token ID.

How large is `vocab_size` in practice? Early models (such as LLaMA 1 and 2) used
smaller vocabularies of 32K tokens. Modern open-weights models have shifted
toward much larger vocabularies to represent multilingual text and code more
compactly.

Throughout the rest of the article, we quote real numbers from two reference
points: Qwen 3.6 and the much larger Kimi K3 2.8T. Qwen 3.6 ships in two
flavors, and the difference matters for the numbers we quote. The **dense** 27B
runs every one of its parameters for every single token. The **sparse** 35B is a
Mixture of Experts model: it carries more parameters in total, but each token
only activates a small slice of them, so the compute per token stays close to
that of a much smaller model.

We use the dense 27B wherever the number does not depend on MoE, and switch to
the sparse 35B once we reach the expert-specific dimensions.

Interestingly, model parameter count does not dictate `vocab_size`: Qwen 3.6 27B
uses a `vocab_size` of 248K, while Kimi K3 2.8T uses 164K. A larger vocabulary
compresses text into fewer tokens, but it also means `embedding_table` has 150K
to 250K rows.

Each embedding vector has a length of `hidden_size`, an important dimension used
throughout the model. Looking up every token ID in the sequence turns the
`[seq_len]` list of IDs into a `[seq_len, hidden_size]` matrix.

Here is what `lookup` and the `embedding` module look like in Python:

```python
def lookup(token_id, embedding_table):
    # token_id: int
    # embedding_table: [vocab_size, hidden_size]
    # token_vec: [hidden_size]
    token_vec = embedding_table[token_id]
    return token_vec

def embedding(input_ids, embedding_table):
    # input_ids: [seq_len]
    # embedding_table: [vocab_size, hidden_size]
    # embed_out: [seq_len, hidden_size]
    embed_out = [lookup(token_id, embedding_table) for token_id in input_ids]
    return embed_out
```


## lm_head

After learning about `embedding`, whose output is fed into `decoder`,
we turn to `lm_head`. It takes the output of the decoder stack (`decoder_out`)
and converts it into `logits`, as shown in the figure below:

[Diagram: The lm_head module takes the final hidden states and predicts next-token logits across the vocabulary. (llm/lm-head-breakdown.svg)]

Just as `embed_out` marks the end of backpropagation, the logits mark its
start.  During training, these logits are compared against the actual next
token (the ground truth) to compute the loss. Backpropagation begins at this
loss, flowing gradients backward through `lm_head`, across all decoder blocks,
and finally into `embedding_table` to update all the learnable weights.

During inference, the model does not compute a loss; instead, `greedy_sampler`
uses the logits directly to pick the next token.

You might notice that the input shape of `decoder` is identical to its
output shape. In other words, the tensor shape `[seq_len, hidden_size]` remains
the same after passing through all the decoder blocks.

How large is `hidden_size` in practice? Unlike `vocab_size`, which is largely
independent of model scale, `hidden_size` grows directly with parameter count.
Smaller models around 7B or 8B typically use a `hidden_size` of 4,096. Moving up
the scale, Qwen 3.6 27B uses 5,120, while Kimi K3 2.8T reaches 7,168.
Wider vectors give the model more capacity to hold rich
representations for each token as they flow through the stack.

Looking inside `lm_head`, it breaks down into three sequential parts: `rms_norm`,
`logits_matmul`, and `slice`:

[Diagram: model.predict -> lm_head<br>lm_head breaks down into three sequential operations. (llm/lm-head-internals.svg)]

Here is what `lm_head` looks like in Python:

```python
def lm_head(decoder_out, gamma, embedding_table_T):
    # decoder_out: [seq_len, hidden_size]
    # gamma: [hidden_size]
    # embedding_table_T: [hidden_size, vocab_size]

    # rms_out: [seq_len, hidden_size]
    rms_out = rms_norm(decoder_out, gamma)
    # all_logits: [seq_len, vocab_size]
    all_logits = logits_matmul(rms_out, embedding_table_T)
    # logits: [vocab_size]
    logits = slice_last(all_logits)
    return logits
```

Let's walk through these three operations one by one.

## rms_norm

Before projecting `decoder_out` to vocabulary logits, `lm_head` first
normalizes the input using `rms_norm` (short for Root Mean Square Normalization,
commonly written as RMSNorm). Because normalization does not change tensor
dimensions, the input and output shapes are identical:

[Diagram: model.predict -> lm_head<br>rms_norm normalizes the input activations while preserving the original tensor shape. (llm/rms-norm-breakdown.svg)]

Zooming into `rms_norm`: it is a token-wise operation, meaning each row of the
input matrix is normalized independently:

[Diagram: model.predict -> lm_head -> rms_norm<br>Inside rms_norm, each token vector is scaled by its root-mean-square norm (circled N) and multiplied elementwise by gamma. (llm/rms-norm-internals.svg)]

Here, `gamma` is the only learnable weight. It has a shape of `[hidden_size]`,
matching the dimension of each token vector. It is multiplied element-wise with
each token vector.

RMSNorm is an improved version of the earlier LayerNorm. It keeps the rescaling
and drops the mean subtraction, which turned out to matter little in practice.

Here is the Python code for `norm_token`, which takes a single token vector and
the learnable weight `gamma`:

```python
EPS = 1e-6

def norm_token(token_vec, gamma):
    # token_vec: [hidden_size]
    sum_of_squares = 0
    for v in token_vec:
        sum_of_squares += v ** 2
    rms = (sum_of_squares / len(token_vec) + EPS) ** 0.5

    # output: [hidden_size]
    output = []
    for i in range(len(token_vec)):
        output.append(token_vec[i] / rms * gamma[i])
    return output

def rms_norm(tensor, gamma):
    # tensor: [seq_len, hidden_size]
    # rms_out: [seq_len, hidden_size]
    rms_out = [norm_token(token_vec, gamma) for token_vec in tensor]
    return rms_out
```

This `rms_norm` module is used throughout the model; we will see it again soon
in the attention and feed-forward blocks.


## logits_matmul

The output of `rms_norm` feeds directly into `logits_matmul`, which performs a
matrix multiplication to produce `all_logits`:

[Diagram: model.predict -> lm_head<br>logits_matmul projects normalized hidden states to vocabulary dimension scores for all tokens. (llm/logits-matmul-breakdown.svg)]

You may notice that the output tensor still has the same number of tokens
(`seq_len`), but the length of each token vector has expanded from
`hidden_size` to `vocab_size`. Each row in `all_logits` is now a vector of
logits, containing an unnormalized prediction score for every token in the
vocabulary (as we introduced in `greedy_sampler`).

Zooming into `logits_matmul`: like `embedding` and `rms_norm`, this is a
token-wise operation. The input matrix splits into individual token vectors.
Each token vector multiplies the weight matrix `embedding_table.T`, and the
resulting vectors are combined back into `all_logits`:

[Diagram: model.predict -> lm_head -> logits_matmul<br>Inside logits_matmul, a matrix multiplication (circled X) projects each token vector against embedding_table.T. (llm/logits-matmul-internals.svg)]

Notice that the learnable weight matrix is the transpose of `embedding_table`.
In the `embedding` step, the table mapped discrete token IDs into dense vectors
of length `hidden_size`. Multiplying by its transpose does the reverse,
projecting each token vector from shape `[hidden_size]` back to `[vocab_size]`.
Reusing the embedding weights here is called **weight tying**, which saves a
significant number of parameters. When weights are untied, models use a
separate projection matrix of shape `[hidden_size, vocab_size]` instead, but the
computation is identical.

Because multiplying a vector by a matrix is used in several places throughout
the model, we write a general `matmul` helper in plain Python. Here is what
`matmul` and `logits_matmul` look like in Python:

```python
def matmul(vec, matrix):
    # vec: [in_dim]
    # matrix: [in_dim, out_dim]
    in_dim = len(vec)
    out_dim = len(matrix[0])
    output = []
    for col in range(out_dim):
        dot_product = sum(vec[k] * matrix[k][col] for k in range(in_dim))
        output.append(dot_product)
    return output

def logits_matmul(rms_out, embedding_table_T):
    # rms_out: [seq_len, hidden_size]
    # embedding_table_T: [hidden_size, vocab_size]

    # all_logits: [seq_len, vocab_size]
    all_logits = [matmul(token_vec, embedding_table_T) for token_vec in rms_out]
    return all_logits
```

## slice

`slice` is the last step in `lm_head`, as well as the final operation inside
`model.predict`.

As we saw earlier, the output of `model.predict` is a single 1D logits vector of
shape `[vocab_size]`. But `logits_matmul` produces `all_logits`, a 2D matrix
containing `seq_len` logit vectors. The job of `slice` is simple: it extracts
the very last vector from the matrix and returns it, as shown in the figure
below:

[Diagram: model.predict -> lm_head -> slice<br>slice extracts the final row of all_logits corresponding to the last token position. (llm/slice-breakdown.svg)]

That final vector provides the scores for the sampler to pick the next token.
Because slicing the last row of a 2D list in Python only requires index `-1`,
the code is straightforward:

```python
def slice_last(all_logits):
    # all_logits: [seq_len, vocab_size]
    # logits: [vocab_size]
    logits = all_logits[-1]
    return logits
```

## decoder

So far, we have explored everything before and after `decoder`:
`embedding` at the input and `lm_head` at the output. Now, we are ready to dive
into the core and most complex part of the Transformer architecture.

As shown in the figure below, the input and output shapes of the module are
identical, `[seq_len, hidden_size]`:

[Diagram: The decoder processes token embeddings through stacked transformer layers. (llm/decoder-breakdown.svg)]

Zooming into `decoder`: it consists of a stack of identical decoder
blocks chained in series, with each block's output feeding directly into the
next:

[Diagram: model.predict -> decoder<br>The decoder consists of a sequential stack of identical decoder_block layers. (llm/decoder-stack.svg)]

As a reference, Qwen 3.6 27B has 64 decoder blocks, and Kimi K3 2.8T has 93 decoder
blocks.

Because each individual block preserves tensor dimensions, the sequence retains
its `[seq_len, hidden_size]` shape from the first block to the last.

Here is what `decoder` looks like in Python:

```python
def decoder(embed_out, decoder_blocks):
    # embed_out: [seq_len, hidden_size]
    # decoder_blocks: list of decoder_block layers

    # decoder_out: [seq_len, hidden_size]
    decoder_out = embed_out
    for decoder_block in decoder_blocks:
        decoder_out = decoder_block(decoder_out)
    return decoder_out
```

## decoder_block

Zooming into a single `decoder_block`: each block contains two sub-layers with
residual connections: grouped query attention (`gqa_block`) and mixture of
experts (`moe_block`). The input passes through `gqa_block` and is added back to
itself element-wise via a residual connection, and that result passes through
`moe_block` and is added back to itself element-wise:

[Diagram: model.predict -> decoder -> decoder_block<br>decoder_block combines a gqa_block and a moe_block, each followed by an elementwise residual addition. (llm/decoder-block-breakdown.svg)]

Because the residual additions are element-wise, the tensor shape
`[seq_len, hidden_size]` remains unchanged through both `gqa_block` and
`moe_block`.

Here is what a single `decoder_block` looks like in Python:

```python
def add(tensor_a, tensor_b):
    # tensor_a: [seq_len, hidden_size]
    # tensor_b: [seq_len, hidden_size]
    seq_len = len(tensor_a)
    hidden_size = len(tensor_a[0])

    # output: [seq_len, hidden_size]
    output = [[0] * hidden_size for _ in range(seq_len)]
    for i in range(seq_len):
        for j in range(hidden_size):
            output[i][j] = tensor_a[i][j] + tensor_b[i][j]
    return output

def decoder_block(decoder_in, gqa_block, moe_block):
    # decoder_in: [seq_len, hidden_size]

    # gqa_out: [seq_len, hidden_size]
    gqa_out = gqa_block(decoder_in)
    residual_1 = add(decoder_in, gqa_out)

    # moe_out: [seq_len, hidden_size]
    moe_out = moe_block(residual_1)

    # decoder_out: [seq_len, hidden_size]
    decoder_out = add(residual_1, moe_out)
    return decoder_out
```


## moe_block

`gqa_block` runs first inside the block, but `moe_block` is the simpler of the
two, so let's start there. As shown in the figure below, the input and
output shapes of the module are identical, `[seq_len, hidden_size]`:

[Diagram: model.predict -> decoder -> decoder_block<br>The moe_block computes mixture-of-experts feedforward updates. (llm/moe-block-breakdown.svg)]

Zooming into `moe_block`: it consists of three steps in sequence: normalizing
tokens with `rms_norm` (which we introduced earlier in `lm_head`), computing
routing weights with `router`, and passing them to `moe` to compute the weighted
expert outputs:

[Diagram: model.predict -> decoder -> decoder_block -> moe_block<br>Inside moe_block, inputs are normalized by rms_norm, routed by router, and processed by the moe module. (llm/moe-block-internals.svg)]

Here is what `moe_block` looks like in Python:

```python
def moe_block(moe_in, rms_norm, router, moe):
    # moe_in: [seq_len, hidden_size]

    # rms_out: [seq_len, hidden_size]
    rms_out = rms_norm(moe_in)

    # top_weights: [seq_len, num_experts]
    top_weights = router(rms_out)

    # moe_out: [seq_len, hidden_size]
    moe_out = moe(rms_out, top_weights)
    return moe_out
```

A new dimension shows up in `top_weights`: `num_experts`. This represents the
total number of expert networks available in the layer. We will dive into how
tokens route to these experts in the next few sections.

Notice that `moe_block` normalizes its input with `rms_norm` right at the
start, before computing routing weights and expert outputs and after the start
of branching out the residual connection. This arrangement is known as
**Pre-LN** (pre-layer normalization).

This technique works hand in hand with the residual connection. Without Pre-LN,
the tensor between the end of one residual connection and the start of the next
would be normalized. Every token would have to pass through that normalization
at each choke point, with no way around it.

With Pre-LN, normalization happens inside the branch between the start and end
of the residual connection. This moves normalization off the model's main choke
points and places it onto a parallel path, leaving the residual stream untouched.

## router

The normalized matrix is fed into `router`, which outputs a matrix called `top_weights`
with shape `[seq_len, num_experts]` as shown in the figure below:

[Diagram: model.predict -> decoder -> decoder_block -> moe_block<br>The router selects the top experts and calculates their gating weights for each token. (llm/router-breakdown.svg)]

`num_experts` is an important hyperparameter here: it sets the number of
subnetworks, also known as experts, in each MoE module. This is where we switch
to the sparse Qwen 3.6 35B, which has 256 experts, while Kimi K3 2.8T uses 896
experts per MoE module.

Zooming into `router`: it is again a token-wise operation. The input matrix splits into
individual token vectors. Each token vector passes through `route_token` (circled as **R**)
along with the weight matrix `w_router` to compute its expert routing weights.
The output row vectors are then stacked back into the matrix `top_weights`:

[Diagram: model.predict -> decoder -> decoder_block -> moe_block -> router<br>Inside router, matrix multiplication and softmax score all experts to produce the top experts and weights. (llm/router-internals.svg)]

Inside `route_token`, we see another important hyperparameter: `TOP_K`. In an MoE
module, we do not activate all `num_experts` for every token. Instead, we only
select the top ones. `TOP_K` is the number of experts we select for each token;
we will see how they compute outputs in the next few sections.

As a reference, Qwen 3.6 35B activates 9 out of 256 experts per token, while Kimi
K3 2.8T activates 16 out of 896 experts per token.

In `route_token`, we first multiply the token vector by the weight matrix
`w_router` to produce a logits vector, where each value corresponds to one
expert.

Then, we construct the `top_weights` vector. We pick the `TOP_K` highest scores
from the logits vector, set the ones not in `TOP_K` to 0, and normalize the
selected scores with a `softmax` function so they sum to 1.

For example, with `TOP_K = 2`, suppose a token produces raw logits `[1.2, 1.6, 0.3]`
for 3 experts. The top two scores are `1.2` (expert 0) and `1.6` (expert 1). Normalizing
them with softmax yields approximately `.4` and `.6`. Setting the unselected expert 2 to 0
gives the final vector `[.4, .6, 0]`, matching the first row of `top_weights` in the diagram
above.

Here is what `route_token` and `router` look like in Python:

```python
import math

TOP_K = 2

def softmax(scores):
    # scores: list of scalars
    max_score = max(scores)
    exp_scores = [math.exp(s - max_score) for s in scores]
    sum_exp = sum(exp_scores)
    return [s / sum_exp for s in exp_scores]

def route_token(token_vec, w_router):
    # token_vec: [hidden_size]
    # w_router:  [hidden_size, num_experts]

    # logits: [num_experts]
    # example value: [1.2, 1.6, 0.3]
    logits = matmul(token_vec, w_router)

    num_experts = len(logits)

    # indices: [num_experts]
    # example value: [0, 1, 2]
    indices = [i for i in range(num_experts)]

    # sorted_indices: [num_experts]
    # example value: [1, 0, 2]
    sorted_indices = sorted(indices, key=lambda i: logits[i], reverse=True)

    # top_indices: [TOP_K]
    # example value: [1, 0]
    top_indices = sorted_indices[:TOP_K]

    # top_logits: [TOP_K]
    # example value: [1.6, 1.2]
    top_logits = [logits[i] for i in top_indices]

    # top_probs: [TOP_K]
    # example value: [0.6, 0.4]
    top_probs = softmax(top_logits)

    # top_weights: [num_experts]
    # example value: [0.4, 0.6, 0]
    top_weights = [0.0] * num_experts
    for k in range(TOP_K):
        top_weights[top_indices[k]] = top_probs[k]
    return top_weights

def router(rms_out, w_router):
    # rms_out: [seq_len, hidden_size]
    # top_weights: [seq_len, num_experts]
    top_weights = [route_token(token_vec, w_router) for token_vec in rms_out]
    return top_weights
```

## moe

`moe` takes the normalized tensor `rms_out` and the router output `top_weights`
as inputs, producing `moe_out` with the exact same shape as `rms_out`:

[Diagram: model.predict -> decoder -> decoder_block -> moe_block<br>The moe module processes token representations through sparse combinations of expert sub-networks. (llm/moe-breakdown.svg)]

To make this easy to follow, we split `rms_out` and `top_weights` into individual
token rows. Taking token 0 as an example, `rms_out_0` and `top_weights_0` are the
corresponding rows. We also split `top_weights_0` into three scalar weights, one
for each expert. Here is how they work together to produce `moe_out_0`:

[Diagram: model.predict -> decoder -> decoder_block -> moe_block -> moe<br>Processing a single token in moe: the token vector passes through its selected experts and is combined using routing weights. (llm/moe-token.svg)]

First, `rms_out_0` feeds into all three experts (`expert_0`, `expert_1`, and
`expert_2`), and each expert produces an output vector of shape `[hidden_size]`.
Next, each output vector is multiplied by its corresponding scalar from
`top_weights_0`. This is an element-wise scalar-vector multiplication, scaling
every element in the vector. Finally, an element-wise add combines the three
scaled vectors into `moe_out_0`.

In this example, `expert_2` is not activated. Its output is multiplied by 0,
producing an all-zero vector that contributes nothing to the element-wise add.
Its weight was set to 0 during routing because it was not among the `TOP_K`
experts for this token.

Here is what `moe_token` and `moe` look like in Python:

```python
def moe_token(token_vec, top_weights, experts):
    # token_vec: [hidden_size]
    # top_weights: [num_experts]
    hidden_size = len(token_vec)

    # moe_out: [hidden_size]
    moe_out = [0.0] * hidden_size
    for i in range(len(experts)):
        # expert_out: [hidden_size]
        expert_out = experts[i](token_vec)
        for j in range(hidden_size):
            moe_out[j] += top_weights[i] * expert_out[j]
    return moe_out

def moe(rms_out, top_weights, experts):
    # rms_out: [seq_len, hidden_size]
    # top_weights: [seq_len, num_experts]

    # moe_out: [seq_len, hidden_size]
    moe_out = [
        moe_token(token_vec, weights, experts)
        for token_vec, weights in zip(rms_out, top_weights)
    ]
    return moe_out
```

We can use the following mental model to understand how the MoE module works
across the full sequence. Each token activates its own top-$k$ experts, and the
selected experts can differ from token to token. Tokens are only routed to these
activated experts, and their outputs are weighted and added together
element-wise to produce `moe_out`:

[Diagram: model.predict -> decoder -> decoder_block -> moe_block -> moe<br>The sequence-level mental model of moe: tokens are dispatched across experts and aggregated into moe_out. (llm/moe-internals.svg)]

This also gives us a neat way to think about the dense models we mentioned
earlier: a dense model is just one big expert that is always activated for every
token.

## expert

Now, we are ready to peek into the last module in MoE: `expert`.
Each expert is a **SwiGLU** (Swish Gated Linear Unit) feed-forward network.
The architecture of an `expert` is shown in the following figure.
Again, for better illustration, we only use a single token as input here:

[Diagram: model.predict -> decoder -> decoder_block -> moe_block -> moe -> expert<br>Inside an expert, a token passes through gate and up projections, silu activation (circled S), and down projection. (llm/expert-internals.svg)]

Each `expert` uses three weight matrices (`w_gate`, `w_up`, and `w_down`) to do the matmuls.

`silu` (marked as **S** in the diagram) is the SiLU (Swish) activation function.
Both `silu` and the element-wise multiplication that follows operate on vectors
element by element without changing their dimensions. Whenever we omit
intermediate output tensors between operations in our diagrams, it means their
shape stays exactly the same as the incoming input tensor, which is
`[inter_size]` here.

The gate is what makes this a SwiGLU rather than a plain feed-forward network,
with `w_up` producing the values and `w_gate` one multiplier for each. Why that
beats the simpler alternatives is still not well understood, and the paper that
introduced these variants is refreshingly blunt about having no explanation
for it[@swiglu].

Here is the Python code for `silu`:

```python
import math

def silu(x):
    return x / (1.0 + math.exp(-x))
```

Using our `matmul` helper, here is what `expert_token` and `expert` look like in
Python:

```python
def expert_token(token_vec, w_gate, w_up, w_down):
    # token_vec: [hidden_size]
    # w_gate, w_up: [hidden_size, inter_size]
    # w_down: [inter_size, hidden_size]

    # x_gate: [inter_size]
    x_gate = matmul(token_vec, w_gate)

    # x_up: [inter_size]
    x_up = matmul(token_vec, w_up)

    # x_act: [inter_size]
    x_act = [silu(x) for x in x_gate]

    # x_inter: [inter_size]
    inter_size = len(x_act)
    x_inter = [x_act[i] * x_up[i] for i in range(inter_size)]

    # x_down: [hidden_size]
    x_down = matmul(x_inter, w_down)
    return x_down

def expert(tensor, w_gate, w_up, w_down):
    # tensor: [seq_len, hidden_size]
    # output: [seq_len, hidden_size]
    output = [expert_token(token_vec, w_gate, w_up, w_down) for token_vec in tensor]
    return output
```

As a reference for the intermediate dimension, Qwen 3.6 35B uses an `inter_size`
of 512 per expert, while Kimi K3 2.8T uses 3,584. In MoE models with
many experts, this inner dimension is often kept relatively narrow for each
individual expert so that activating multiple experts per token remains
computationally efficient.

## gqa_block

So far, we have covered `moe_block`, which forms the second half of a single `decoder_block`.
The first half is `gqa_block`.
Here, `gqa` stands for **Grouped-Query Attention** (GQA), a modern evolution of the
multi-head attention mechanism introduced in the original Transformer paper. We will
see how it works in detail in the next few sections. As shown in the following
figure, the input and output shapes are identical (`[seq_len, hidden_size]`):

[Diagram: model.predict -> decoder -> decoder_block<br>The gqa_block computes grouped-query attention. (llm/gqa-block-breakdown.svg)]

Zooming into `gqa_block`: it consists of three steps in sequence: `rms_norm`, `gqa`, and `out_matmul`:

[Diagram: model.predict -> decoder -> decoder_block -> gqa_block<br>Inside gqa_block, the input passes through rms_norm, the gqa attention mechanism, and out_matmul. (llm/gqa-block-internals.svg)]

Here is what `gqa_block` looks like in Python:

```python
def gqa_block(gqa_block_in, rms_norm, gqa, out_matmul):
    # gqa_block_in: [seq_len, hidden_size]

    # rms_out: [seq_len, hidden_size]
    rms_out = rms_norm(gqa_block_in)

    # gqa_out: [seq_len, hidden_size]
    gqa_out = gqa(rms_out)

    # gqa_block_out: [seq_len, hidden_size]
    gqa_block_out = out_matmul(gqa_out)
    return gqa_block_out
```

Notice that each sub-module inside `gqa_block` shares the exact same input and output shape (`[seq_len, hidden_size]`).

Just like `moe_block`, `gqa_block` follows the Pre-LN design. It normalizes its
input with `rms_norm` after the residual connection has branched out. This keeps
normalization off the choke point, leaving the main residual stream unnormalized as
it passes through the block.

Because `rms_norm` is identical to what we explored in `lm_head` and `moe_block`,
we can jump straight into `out_matmul` and `gqa`.

## out_matmul

Let's look at `out_matmul` first. It is the simpler of the two remaining components:
just a standard projection that maps the concatenated attention output back to the
residual stream. `out_matmul` takes the output of `gqa` (`gqa_out`) and produces
`gqa_block_out` with the exact same shape:

[Diagram: model.predict -> decoder -> decoder_block -> gqa_block<br>out_matmul projects the concatenated attention group outputs back to the hidden size dimension. (llm/out-matmul-breakdown.svg)]

Zooming into `out_matmul`: like `rms_norm` and `logits_matmul`, this is a token-wise
operation. The input matrix splits into individual token vectors, each multiplying
the weight matrix `w_matmul`, and the resulting vectors combine back into `gqa_block_out`:

[Diagram: model.predict -> decoder -> decoder_block -> gqa_block -> out_matmul<br>Inside out_matmul, matrix multiplication (circled X) multiplies gqa_out by the output projection weights w_matmul. (llm/out-matmul-internals.svg)]

Because each token vector simply multiplies `w_matmul`, we can reuse the `matmul`
helper subroutine from the `expert` section:

```python
def out_matmul(gqa_out, w_matmul):
    # gqa_out: [seq_len, hidden_size]
    # w_matmul: [hidden_size, hidden_size]

    # gqa_block_out: [seq_len, hidden_size]
    gqa_block_out = [matmul(token_vec, w_matmul) for token_vec in gqa_out]
    return gqa_block_out
```

## gqa

`gqa` takes the normalized tokens `rms_out` and produces `gqa_out`, which feeds directly into `out_matmul`.
Its input and output share the exact same shape, `[seq_len, hidden_size]`:

[Diagram: model.predict -> decoder -> decoder_block -> gqa_block<br>The gqa module splits attention computation into independent head groups. (llm/gqa-breakdown.svg)]

Zooming into `gqa`: the attention computation is divided into independent head groups
(`group_0`, `group_1`, and `group_2`). To clearly illustrate how the dimensions
and projections work in this module and the upcoming `group_0` section, we
expand the visual representation of `hidden_size` from 3 cells to 12 cells.

Each group receives the full `rms_out` matrix of shape `[seq_len,
hidden_size]`. Inside each group, the tokens are projected into Query, Key, and
Value representations, and the group produces an output matrix of shape
`[seq_len, head_dim]` (where `head_dim = hidden_size // num_groups`). Finally,
the outputs from all groups are concatenated back along the column dimension to
form `gqa_out`:

[Diagram: model.predict -> decoder -> decoder_block -> gqa_block -> gqa<br>Inside gqa, inputs are processed in parallel across attention groups and concatenated into gqa_out. (llm/gqa-internals.svg)]

Here is what `gqa` looks like in Python:

```python
def gqa(rms_out, groups):
    # rms_out: [seq_len, hidden_size]
    seq_len = len(rms_out)

    # Each group computes attention on the full rms_out input
    # group_out: [seq_len, head_dim]
    group_outs = [group(rms_out) for group in groups]

    # Concatenate group outputs back along the column dimension
    # gqa_out: [seq_len, hidden_size]
    gqa_out = []
    # Iterate over the rows of gqa_out
    for t in range(seq_len):
        row = []
        # Iterate over groups to concatenate the outputs
        for out in group_outs:
            row.extend(out[t])
        gqa_out.append(row)
    return gqa_out
```

Here we introduce a new hyperparameter, `num_groups`, as well as `head_dim`, which
depends on it: `head_dim = hidden_size // num_groups`. As a reference, Qwen 3.6 27B
has 4 groups, while Kimi K3 2.8T uses a different attention architecture entirely.

## group_0

Zooming into `group_0`: it takes the full `rms_out` matrix and projects it into
query (`q`), key (`k`), and value (`v`) tensors with matmul using the learned
weights `w_q`, `w_k`, and `w_v`. Note that these matmuls are also token-wise operations.

Next, `q` and `k` pass through `rope` (circled as **P**), while `v` remains unchanged.
Then, all three branches feed into `attention_head` (circled as **H**) to
produce the final output, `group_0_out` of shape `[seq_len, head_dim]`:

[Diagram: model.predict -> decoder -> decoder_block -> gqa_block -> gqa -> group_0<br>Inside group_0, inputs project to q, k, and v, apply rotary embedding (circled P), and enter multi-head attention (circled H). (llm/group-0-internals.svg)]

As you can see, `w_q` has an extra depth axis (the z-axis in our diagram), so its
output also has a z-axis. We call each matrix along this depth axis a head. In
`group_0`, we have one `k` head and one `v` head, but multiple `q` heads. The
length of this z-axis is the number of query heads, `q_heads`.

This introduces another hyperparameter: `d_head`, the length of each token vector
in `q`, `k`, and `v`. Once you choose `d_head`, the number of query heads `q_heads`
is decided as well. That is because `attention_head` concatenates all `q_heads`
outputs along their channel dimension into the group output `head_dim`:

$$
\text{head_dim} = \text{q_heads} \times \text{d_head}
$$

In production configurations, architects usually define this in reverse: they
pick the total number of attention heads first and derive
`d_head = hidden_size // num_attention_heads`.

For comparison, Qwen 3.6 27B uses 6 query heads per group.

Here is what `group_0` looks like in Python:

```python
def group_0(rms_out, w_q, w_k, w_v):
    # rms_out: [seq_len, hidden_size]
    # w_q: [q_heads, hidden_size, d_head]
    # w_k: [hidden_size, d_head]
    # w_v: [hidden_size, d_head]

    # Project inputs to q, k, v token-wise using our matmul helper
    # q: [q_heads, seq_len, d_head]
    # k: [seq_len, d_head]
    # v: [seq_len, d_head]
    q = [[matmul(token_vec, w) for token_vec in rms_out] for w in w_q]
    k = [matmul(token_vec, w_k) for token_vec in rms_out]
    v = [matmul(token_vec, w_v) for token_vec in rms_out]

    # Encode positions with rotary embedding
    # rope is token-wise and preserves tensor shape
    q = rope(q)
    k = rope(k)

    # Compute multi-head attention and concatenate heads
    # group_0_out: [seq_len, head_dim]
    group_0_out = attention_head(q, k, v)
    return group_0_out
```

Even though `rope` and `attention_head` are stateless functions, both are central
to how attention works. Let's dive into them one by one.

## rope

`rope` (circled as **P**) is short for **Rotary Position Embedding**.
Earlier transformer architectures injected position information right at the
start of the model. Modern LLMs instead move position encoding directly
into the attention layer. Notice that only `q` and `k` go through `rope`,
while `v` skips `rope` entirely.

`rope` is a token-wise operation: each token vector is processed independently
based on its position index, without mixing information across different tokens
in the sequence.

In `group_0`, `k` is a 2D matrix (`[seq_len, d_head]`), while `q` is a 3D tensor
with multiple query heads (`[q_heads, seq_len, d_head]`). The entry-point `rope`
function inspects the input shape and routes the tensor to either `rope_2d` or
`rope_3d`:

```python
def rope(x):
    # x: [seq_len, d_head] or [q_heads, seq_len, d_head]
    if isinstance(x[0][0], list):
        return rope_3d(x)
    return rope_2d(x)
```

Both functions handle tensor dimensions by calling a token-level subroutine,
`rope_token`. `rope_2d` processes each token vector across the sequence, while
`rope_3d` passes each head matrix into `rope_2d`:

```python
def rope_2d(x):
    # x: [seq_len, d_head]
    # return: [seq_len, d_head]
    return [rope_token(token_vec, pos) for pos, token_vec in enumerate(x)]

def rope_3d(x):
    # x: [q_heads, seq_len, d_head]
    # return: [q_heads, seq_len, d_head]
    return [rope_2d(head) for head in x]
```

Inside `rope_token`, the vector is processed two numbers at a time. It steps
through consecutive pairs along the token vector, passing each pair together
with its token position to `rope_pair`:

```python
def rope_token(token_vec, pos):
    # token_vec: [d_head]
    # pos: scalar
    d_head = len(token_vec)
    # output: [d_head]
    output = []
    # Iterate over consecutive coordinate pairs: (x0, x1), (x2, x3), ...
    for i in range(0, d_head, 2):
        r0, r1 = rope_pair(token_vec[i], token_vec[i + 1], pos, i, d_head)
        output.append(r0)
        output.append(r1)
    return output
```

Finally, `rope_pair` operates on two individual numbers. It updates the pair
based on the coordinates of `x0` and `x1` on the matrix (token position `pos`
and the dimension index `i`), returning two modified values. The operations here
are all on scalars. Because the angle is proportional to position, the two
rotations cancel down to a difference in the later dot product, so attention
sees relative position. Feel free to dive deeper on your own.

```python
import math

def rope_pair(x0, x1, pos, i, d_head):
    # The variables in this function are all scalars.
    freq = 1.0 / (10000 ** (i / d_head))
    angle = pos * freq
    cos_val = math.cos(angle)
    sin_val = math.sin(angle)
    return x0 * cos_val - x1 * sin_val, x0 * sin_val + x1 * cos_val
```

Because `rope` preserves tensor shapes, `q` and `k` emerge with the exact same
dimensions they had before entering `rope`, ready for `attention_head`.

## attention_head

The attention head circled as **H** takes the query tensor `q`, key `k`, and value `v`.
This is the only operation in the LLM that is not a token-wise operation.
We have to pass in all the tokens at once instead of one by one.
This is the most complex function we need to explain in this article.

Remember that the `q` tensor has a z-axis of length `q_heads`?
In the `attention_head` function, we loop over that dimension, calling the
subroutine `dot_product_attention` (marked as **D** in the figure below), which
processes a single 2D query matrix alongside the shared key and value matrices.
Notice in the figure that `q` is the only tensor that splits. Every head reads
the same `k` and `v`. We then concatenate the outputs back into one tensor of
shape `[seq_len, head_dim]`, marked as **C**:

[Diagram: model.predict -> decoder -> decoder_block -> gqa_block -> gqa -> group_0 -> attention_head<br>The query tensor splits into one matrix per head, while the same key and value matrices feed every head. (llm/attention-head-internals.svg)]

```python
def attention_head(q, k, v):
    # q: [q_heads, seq_len, d_head]
    # k: [seq_len, d_head]
    # v: [seq_len, d_head]
    seq_len = len(k)

    # Compute attention for each query head
    # head_outs: [q_heads, seq_len, d_head]
    head_outs = []
    for q_head in q:
        # head_out: [seq_len, d_head]
        head_out = dot_product_attention(q_head, k, v)
        head_outs.append(head_out)

    # Concatenate all head outputs
    # out: [seq_len, head_dim]
    out = []
    for t in range(seq_len):
        # token_out: [head_dim]
        # head_dim == q_heads * d_head
        token_out = []
        for head_out in head_outs:
            # head_out: [seq_len, d_head]
            token_out.extend(head_out[t])
        out.append(token_out)
    return out
```

Zooming into `dot_product_attention`: this subroutine was also used by
traditional multi-head attention (**MHA**) before GQA was introduced. It takes
care of one Q, K, and V head. The function first transposes `k` into `k_T` so
that we can compute dot products between `q_head` and the keys with `matmul`.
Because more operations follow the dot products, we iterate over the tokens
(rows) in `q_head` and handle them one by one. For each token, it delegates the
computation to a token-level subroutine, `attention_token`, and appends the
resulting vector to `head_out`.

The figure below unrolls that loop and shows all three tokens at once. Every row
of `q_head` takes its own trip through the same steps, and the shared `k_T` and
`v` feed all of them. Stack the resulting attention weights and you get a
triangle, because a token is only allowed to look at itself and the tokens
before it:

[Diagram: model.predict -> decoder -> decoder_block -> gqa_block -> gqa -> group_0 -> attention_head -> dot_product_attention<br>Each token attends only to itself and the tokens before it, so the attention weights form a triangle. (llm/dot-product-attention-internals.svg)]

```python
def dot_product_attention(q_head, k, v):
    # q_head: [seq_len, d_head]
    # k: [seq_len, d_head]
    # v: [seq_len, d_head]
    seq_len = len(k)
    d_head = len(k[0])

    # Transpose k to compute dot products with q: [d_head, seq_len]
    k_T = [[k[row][col] for row in range(seq_len)] for col in range(d_head)]

    # head_out: [seq_len, d_head]
    head_out = []
    for i, q_token in enumerate(q_head):
        # token_out: [d_head]
        token_out = attention_token(q_token, k_T, v, i)
        head_out.append(token_out)
    return head_out
```

Finally, `attention_token` performs scaled dot-product attention for a single
token. It first computes dot products with `k_T` to produce a vector of shape
`[seq_len]`. Those scores are then scaled and converted to attention weights,
`weights`, before multiplying with `v`.

To keep generation autoregressive, only the first `i + 1` values in `weights`
(from position 0 up to and including current position `i`) are non-zero.
The remaining future positions are padded with zeros:

```python
import math

def attention_token(q_token, k_T, v, i):
    # q_token: [d_head]
    # k_T: [d_head, seq_len]
    # v: [seq_len, d_head]
    d_head = len(q_token)
    seq_len = len(v)

    # Compute raw dot products against all keys: [seq_len]
    dot_products = matmul(q_token, k_T)

    # Scale scores up to the current token position i: [i + 1]
    scores = []
    for j in range(i + 1):
        scores.append(dot_products[j] / math.sqrt(d_head))

    # weights: [seq_len]
    # Pad zeros for future tokens to make length [seq_len]
    weights = softmax(scores) + [0.0] * (seq_len - (i + 1))

    # Compute weighted sum of values: [d_head]
    token_out = matmul(weights, v)
    return token_out
```

## Putting it all together

We put everything together in [this figure](/the-anatomy-of-an-llm/graph/) to
show the end-to-end workflow of `model.predict`. You can hover over any tensor
to see its name and shape, or any operation to see its Python code. In the
code popups, we used NumPy operations without explicit token-wise iterations to
make them concise and easier to read. You can bookmark the page and come back to
it anytime you need a quick reference.

You can also explore the complete, runnable Python implementation in the
[readable-llm](https://github.com/haifeng-jin/readable-llm) repository on GitHub.
To check that the architecture actually works, we trained a 0.000005B model
(4,596 parameters) on a single sentence. It can only answer the one prompt
`"What is 1+1?"`, which is all we needed. The training code is in the repo too,
if you want to see how those weights were produced.


## Where to go next

What we built here is a foundation. Most models you will run into are variations
on the same shape, and they get much easier to read once you know the baseline.
From here you can branch off in whatever direction interests you: other
architectures, the theory behind why any of this works, or the performance
engineering that separates code written to be read from code written to be fast.
